<dd><font SIZE="-1">URL</font> of the page that will return the <font SIZE="-1">UTC</font> timestamp in <font SIZE="-1">ISO</font> format. Example: ``<a rel="nofollow" HREF="https://time.akamai.com/?iso''">https://time.akamai.com/?iso''</a>
<dt><b>-adaptation_sets</b> <i>adaptation_sets</i>
<dd>Assign streams to AdaptationSets. Syntax is ``id=x,streams=a,b,c id=y,streams=d,e'' with x and y being the IDs of the adaptation sets and a,b,c,d and e are the indices of the mapped streams. 

 To map all video (or audio) streams to an AdaptationSet, ``v'' (or ``a'') can be used as stream identifier instead of IDs. 

 When no assignment is defined, this defaults to an AdaptationSet for each stream.</dl><h3>framecrc</h3>Per-packet <font SIZE="-1">CRC</font> (Cyclic Redundancy Check) testing format. 

 This muxer computes and prints the Adler-32 <font SIZE="-1">CRC</font> for each audio and video packet. By default audio frames are converted to signed 16-bit raw audio and video frames to raw video before computing the <font SIZE="-1">CRC.</font> 

 The output of the muxer consists of a line for each audio and video packet of the form: 

 <pre> &lt;stream_index&gt;, &lt;packet_dts&gt;, &lt;packet_pts&gt;, &lt;packet_duration&gt;, &lt;packet_size&gt;, 0x&lt;CRC&gt;</pre><i></i><font SIZE="-1"><i>CRC</i></font><i></i> is a hexadecimal number 0-padded to 8 digits containing the <font SIZE="-1">CRC</font> of the packet. 

 <i>Examples</i> 

 For example to compute the <font SIZE="-1">CRC</font> of the audio and video frames in <i></i><font SIZE="-1"><i>INPUT</i></font><i></i>, converted to raw audio and video packets, and store it in the file <i>out.crc</i>: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i INPUT -f framecrc out.crc</pre>To print the information to stdout, use the command: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i INPUT -f framecrc -</pre>With <b>ffmpeg</b>, you can select the output format to which the audio and video frames are encoded before computing the <font SIZE="-1">CRC</font> for each packet by specifying the audio and video codec. For example, to compute the <font SIZE="-1">CRC</font> of each decoded input audio frame converted to <font SIZE="-1">PCM</font> unsigned 8-bit and of each decoded input video frame converted to <font SIZE="-1">MPEG-2</font> video, use the command: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i INPUT -c:a pcm_u8 -c:v mpeg2video -f framecrc -</pre>See also the <b>crc</b> muxer.
<h3>framehash</h3>Per-packet hash testing format. 

 This muxer computes and prints a cryptographic hash for each audio and video packet. This can be used for packet-by-packet equality checks without having to individually do a binary comparison on each. 

 By default audio frames are converted to signed 16-bit raw audio and video frames to raw video before computing the hash, but the output of explicit conversions to other codecs can also be used. It uses the <font SIZE="-1">SHA-256</font> cryptographic hash function by default, but supports several other algorithms. 

 The output of the muxer consists of a line for each audio and video packet of the form: 

 <pre> &lt;stream_index&gt;, &lt;packet_dts&gt;, &lt;packet_pts&gt;, &lt;packet_duration&gt;, &lt;packet_size&gt;, &lt;hash&gt;</pre><i>hash</i> is a hexadecimal number representing the computed hash for the packet.
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>hash</b> <i>algorithm</i>
<dd>Use the cryptographic hash function specified by the string <i>algorithm</i>. Supported values include <tt>&quot;MD5&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;murmur3&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;RIPEMD128&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;RIPEMD160&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;RIPEMD256&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;RIPEMD320&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;SHA160&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;SHA224&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;SHA256&quot;</tt> (default), <tt>&quot;SHA512/224&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;SHA512/256&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;SHA384&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;SHA512&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;CRC32&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;adler32&quot;</tt>.</dl>
 

 <i>Examples</i> 

 To compute the <font SIZE="-1">SHA-256</font> hash of the audio and video frames in <i></i><font SIZE="-1"><i>INPUT</i></font><i></i>, converted to raw audio and video packets, and store it in the file <i>out.sha256</i>: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i INPUT -f framehash out.sha256</pre>To print the information to stdout, using the <font SIZE="-1">MD5</font> hash function, use the command: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i INPUT -f framehash -hash md5 -</pre>See also the <b>hash</b> muxer.
<h3>framemd5</h3>Per-packet <font SIZE="-1">MD5</font> testing format. 

 This is a variant of the <b>framehash</b> muxer. Unlike that muxer, it defaults to using the <font SIZE="-1">MD5</font> hash function. 

 <i>Examples</i> 

 To compute the <font SIZE="-1">MD5</font> hash of the audio and video frames in <i></i><font SIZE="-1"><i>INPUT</i></font><i></i>, converted to raw audio and video packets, and store it in the file <i>out.md5</i>: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i INPUT -f framemd5 out.md5</pre>To print the information to stdout, use the command: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i INPUT -f framemd5 -</pre>See also the <b>framehash</b> and <b>md5</b> muxers.
<h3>gif</h3>Animated <font SIZE="-1">GIF</font> muxer. 

 It accepts the following options:
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>loop</b>
<dd>Set the number of times to loop the output. Use <tt>&quot;-1&quot;</tt> for no loop, <tt>0</tt> for looping indefinitely (default).
<dt><b>final_delay</b>
<dd>Force the delay (expressed in centiseconds) after the last frame. Each frame ends with a delay until the next frame. The default is <tt>&quot;-1&quot;</tt>, which is a special value to tell the muxer to re-use the previous delay. In case of a loop, you might want to customize this value to mark a pause for instance.</dl>
 

 For example, to encode a gif looping 10 times, with a 5 seconds delay between the loops: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i INPUT -loop 10 -final_delay 500 out.gif</pre>Note 1: if you wish to extract the frames into separate <font SIZE="-1">GIF</font> files, you need to force the <b>image2</b> muxer: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i INPUT -c:v gif -f image2 &quot;out%d.gif&quot;</pre>Note 2: the <font SIZE="-1">GIF</font> format has a very large time base: the delay between two frames can therefore not be smaller than one centi second.
<h3>hash</h3>Hash testing format. 

 This muxer computes and prints a cryptographic hash of all the input audio and video frames. This can be used for equality checks without having to do a complete binary comparison. 

 By default audio frames are converted to signed 16-bit raw audio and video frames to raw video before computing the hash, but the output of explicit conversions to other codecs can also be used. Timestamps are ignored. It uses the <font SIZE="-1">SHA-256</font> cryptographic hash function by default, but supports several other algorithms. 

 The output of the muxer consists of a single line of the form: <i>algo</i>=<i>hash</i>, where <i>algo</i> is a short string representing the hash function used, and <i>hash</i> is a hexadecimal number representing the computed hash.
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>hash</b> <i>algorithm</i>
<dd>Use the cryptographic hash function specified by the string <i>algorithm</i>. Supported values include <tt>&quot;MD5&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;murmur3&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;RIPEMD128&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;RIPEMD160&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;RIPEMD256&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;RIPEMD320&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;SHA160&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;SHA224&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;SHA256&quot;</tt> (default), <tt>&quot;SHA512/224&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;SHA512/256&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;SHA384&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;SHA512&quot;</tt>, <tt>&quot;CRC32&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;adler32&quot;</tt>.</dl>
 

 <i>Examples</i> 

 To compute the <font SIZE="-1">SHA-256</font> hash of the input converted to raw audio and video, and store it in the file <i>out.sha256</i>: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i INPUT -f hash out.sha256</pre>To print an <font SIZE="-1">MD5</font> hash to stdout use the command: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i INPUT -f hash -hash md5 -</pre>See also the <b>framehash</b> muxer.
<h3>hls</h3>Apple <font SIZE="-1">HTTP</font> Live Streaming muxer that segments MPEG-TS according to the <font SIZE="-1">HTTP</font> Live Streaming (<font SIZE="-1">HLS</font>) specification. 

 It creates a playlist file, and one or more segment files. The output filename specifies the playlist filename. 

 By default, the muxer creates a file for each segment produced. These files have the same name as the playlist, followed by a sequential number and a .ts extension. 

 For example, to convert an input file with <b>ffmpeg</b>: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i in.nut out.m3u8</pre>This example will produce the playlist, <i>out.m3u8</i>, and segment files: <i>out0.ts</i>, <i>out1.ts</i>, <i>out2.ts</i>, etc. 

 See also the <b>segment</b> muxer, which provides a more generic and flexible implementation of a segmenter, and can be used to perform <font SIZE="-1">HLS</font> segmentation. 

 <i>Options</i> 

 This muxer supports the following options:
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>hls_init_time</b> <i>seconds</i>
<dd>Set the initial target segment length in seconds. Default value is <i>0</i>. Segment will be cut on the next key frame after this time has passed on the first m3u8 list. After the initial playlist is filled <b>ffmpeg</b> will cut segments at duration equal to <tt>&quot;hls_time&quot;</tt>
<dt><b>hls_time</b> <i>seconds</i>
<dd>Set the target segment length in seconds. Default value is 2. Segment will be cut on the next key frame after this time has passed.
<dt><b>hls_list_size</b> <i>size</i>
<dd>Set the maximum number of playlist entries. If set to 0 the list file will contain all the segments. Default value is 5.
<dt><b>hls_ts_options</b> <i>options_list</i>
<dd>Set output format options using a :-separated list of key=value parameters. Values containing <tt>&quot;:&quot;</tt> special characters must be escaped.
<dt><b>hls_wrap</b> <i>wrap</i>
<dd>This is a deprecated option, you can use <tt>&quot;hls_list_size&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;hls_flags delete_segments&quot;</tt> instead it 

 This option is useful to avoid to fill the disk with many segment files, and limits the maximum number of segment files written to disk to <i>wrap</i>.
<dt><b>hls_start_number_source</b>
<dd>Start the playlist sequence number (<tt>&quot;#EXT-X-MEDIA-SEQUENCE&quot;</tt>) according to the specified source. Unless <tt>&quot;hls_flags single_file&quot;</tt> is set, it also specifies source of starting sequence numbers of segment and subtitle filenames. In any case, if <tt>&quot;hls_flags append_list&quot;</tt> is set and read playlist sequence number is greater than the specified start sequence number, then that value will be used as start value. 

 It accepts the following values:
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt><b>generic (default)</b>
<dd>Set the starting sequence numbers according to <i>start_number</i> option value.
<dt><b>epoch</b>
<dd>The start number will be the seconds since epoch (1970-01-01 00:00:00)
<dt><b>datetime</b>
<dd>The start number will be based on the current date/time as YYYYmmddHHMMSS. e.g. 20161231235759.</dl></dl><dl COMPACT><dd></dl><dt><b>start_number</b> <i>number</i>
<dd>Start the playlist sequence number (<tt>&quot;#EXT-X-MEDIA-SEQUENCE&quot;</tt>) from the specified <i>number</i> when <i>hls_start_number_source</i> value is <i>generic</i>. (This is the default case.) Unless <tt>&quot;hls_flags single_file&quot;</tt> is set, it also specifies starting sequence numbers of segment and subtitle filenames. Default value is 0.
<dt><b>hls_allow_cache</b> <i>allowcache</i>
<dd>Explicitly set whether the client <font SIZE="-1">MAY</font> (1) or <font SIZE="-1">MUST NOT</font> (0) cache media segments.
<dt><b>hls_base_url</b> <i>baseurl</i>
<dd>Append <i>baseurl</i> to every entry in the playlist. Useful to generate playlists with absolute paths. 

 Note that the playlist sequence number must be unique for each segment and it is not to be confused with the segment filename sequence number which can be cyclic, for example if the <b>wrap</b> option is specified.
<dt><b>hls_segment_filename</b> <i>filename</i>
<dd>Set the segment filename. Unless <tt>&quot;hls_flags single_file&quot;</tt> is set, <i>filename</i> is used as a string format with the segment number: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i in.nut -hls_segment_filename 'file%03d.ts' out.m3u8</pre>This example will produce the playlist, <i>out.m3u8</i>, and segment files: <i>file000.ts</i>, <i>file001.ts</i>, <i>file002.ts</i>, etc. 

 <i>filename</i> may contain full path or relative path specification, but only the file name part without any path info will be contained in the m3u8 segment list. Should a relative path be specified, the path of the created segment files will be relative to the current working directory. When use_localtime_mkdir is set, the whole expanded value of <i>filename</i> will be written into the m3u8 segment list.
<dt><b>use_localtime</b>
<dd>Use <i>strftime()</i> on <i>filename</i> to expand the segment filename with localtime. The segment number is also available in this mode, but to use it, you need to specify second_level_segment_index hls_flag and %%d will be the specifier. 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i in.nut -use_localtime 1 -hls_segment_filename 'file-%Y%m%d-%s.ts' out.m3u8</pre>This example will produce the playlist, <i>out.m3u8</i>, and segment files: <i>file-20160215-1455569023.ts</i>, <i>file-20160215-1455569024.ts</i>, etc. Note: On some systems/environments, the <tt>%s</tt> specifier is not available. See 
&nbsp;<wbr>&nbsp;<tt>&quot;strftime()&quot;</tt>&nbsp;documentation. 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i in.nut -use_localtime 1 -hls_flags second_level_segment_index -hls_segment_filename 'file-%Y%m%d-%%04d.ts' out.m3u8</pre>This example will produce the playlist, <i>out.m3u8</i>, and segment files: <i>file-20160215-0001.ts</i>, <i>file-20160215-0002.ts</i>, etc.
<dt><b>use_localtime_mkdir</b>
<dd>Used together with -use_localtime, it will create all subdirectories which is expanded in <i>filename</i>. 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i in.nut -use_localtime 1 -use_localtime_mkdir 1 -hls_segment_filename '%Y%m%d/file-%Y%m%d-%s.ts' out.m3u8</pre>This example will create a directory 201560215 (if it does not exist), and then produce the playlist, <i>out.m3u8</i>, and segment files: <i>20160215/file-20160215-1455569023.ts</i>, <i>20160215/file-20160215-1455569024.ts</i>, etc. 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i in.nut -use_localtime 1 -use_localtime_mkdir 1 -hls_segment_filename '%Y/%m/%d/file-%Y%m%d-%s.ts' out.m3u8</pre>This example will create a directory hierarchy 2016/02/15 (if any of them do not exist), and then produce the playlist, <i>out.m3u8</i>, and segment files: <i>2016/02/15/file-20160215-1455569023.ts</i>, <i>2016/02/15/file-20160215-1455569024.ts</i>, etc.
<dt><b>hls_key_info_file</b> <i>key_info_file</i>
<dd>Use the information in <i>key_info_file</i> for segment encryption. The first line of <i>key_info_file</i> specifies the key <font SIZE="-1">URI</font> written to the playlist. The key <font SIZE="-1">URL</font> is used to access the encryption key during playback. The second line specifies the path to the key file used to obtain the key during the encryption process. The key file is read as a single packed array of 16 octets in binary format. The optional third line specifies the initialization vector (<font SIZE="-1">IV</font>) as a hexadecimal string to be used instead of the segment sequence number (default) for encryption. Changes to <i>key_info_file</i> will result in segment encryption with the new key/IV and an entry in the playlist for the new key <font SIZE="-1">URI/IV</font> if <tt>&quot;hls_flags periodic_rekey&quot;</tt> is enabled. 

 Key info file format: 

 <pre> &lt;key URI&gt;
 &lt;key file path&gt;
 &lt;IV&gt; (optional)</pre>Example key URIs: 

 <pre> <a rel="nofollow" HREF="http://server/file.key">http://server/file.key</a>
 /path/to/file.key
 file.key</pre>Example key file paths: 

 <pre> file.key
 /path/to/file.key</pre>Example <font SIZE="-1">IV:</font> 

 <pre> 0123456789ABCDEF0123456789ABCDEF</pre>Key info file example: 

 <pre> <a rel="nofollow" HREF="http://server/file.key">http://server/file.key</a>
 /path/to/file.key
 0123456789ABCDEF0123456789ABCDEF</pre>Example shell script: 

 <pre> #!/bin/sh
 BASE_URL=${1:-'.'}
 openssl rand 16 &gt; file.key
 echo $BASE_URL/file.key &gt; file.keyinfo
 echo file.key &gt;&gt; file.keyinfo
 echo $(openssl rand -hex 16) &gt;&gt; file.keyinfo
 ffmpeg -f lavfi -re -i testsrc -c:v h264 -hls_flags delete_segments \
 -hls_key_info_file file.keyinfo out.m3u8</pre><dt><b>-hls_enc</b> <i>enc</i>
<dd>Enable (1) or disable (0) the <font SIZE="-1">AES128</font> encryption. When enabled every segment generated is encrypted and the encryption key is saved as <i>playlist name</i>.key.
<dt><b>-hls_enc_key</b> <i>key</i>
<dd>Hex-coded 16byte key to encrypt the segments, by default it is randomly generated.
<dt><b>-hls_enc_key_url</b> <i>keyurl</i>
<dd>If set, <i>keyurl</i> is prepended instead of <i>baseurl</i> to the key filename in the playlist.
<dt><b>-hls_enc_iv</b> <i>iv</i>
<dd>Hex-coded 16byte initialization vector for every segment instead of the autogenerated ones.
<dt><b>hls_segment_type</b> <i>flags</i>
<dd>Possible values:
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt><b>mpegts</b>
<dd>If this flag is set, the hls segment files will format to mpegts. the mpegts files is used in all hls versions.
<dt><b>fmp4</b>
<dd>If this flag is set, the hls segment files will format to fragment mp4 looks like dash. the fmp4 files is used in hls after version 7.</dl></dl><dl COMPACT><dd></dl><dt><b>hls_fmp4_init_filename</b> <i>filename</i>
<dd>set filename to the fragment files header file, default filename is <i>init.mp4</i>.
<dt><b>hls_flags</b> <i>flags</i>
<dd>Possible values:
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt><b>single_file</b>
<dd>If this flag is set, the muxer will store all segments in a single MPEG-TS file, and will use byte ranges in the playlist. <font SIZE="-1">HLS</font> playlists generated with this way will have the version number 4. For example: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i in.nut -hls_flags single_file out.m3u8</pre>Will produce the playlist, <i>out.m3u8</i>, and a single segment file, <i>out.ts</i>.
<dt><b>delete_segments</b>
<dd>Segment files removed from the playlist are deleted after a period of time equal to the duration of the segment plus the duration of the playlist.
<dt><b>append_list</b>
<dd>Append new segments into the end of old segment list, and remove the <tt>&quot;#EXT-X-ENDLIST&quot;</tt> from the old segment list.
<dt><b>round_durations</b>
<dd>Round the duration info in the playlist file segment info to integer values, instead of using floating point.
<dt><b>discont_start</b>
<dd>Add the <tt>&quot;#EXT-X-DISCONTINUITY&quot;</tt> tag to the playlist, before the first segment's information.
<dt><b>omit_endlist</b>
<dd>Do not append the <tt>&quot;EXT-X-ENDLIST&quot;</tt> tag at the end of the playlist.
<dt><b>periodic_rekey</b>
<dd>The file specified by <tt>&quot;hls_key_info_file&quot;</tt> will be checked periodically and detect updates to the encryption info. Be sure to replace this file atomically, including the file containing the <font SIZE="-1">AES</font> encryption key.
<dt><b>split_by_time</b>
<dd>Allow segments to start on frames other than keyframes. This improves behavior on some players when the time between keyframes is inconsistent, but may make things worse on others, and can cause some oddities during seeking. This flag should be used with the <tt>&quot;hls_time&quot;</tt> option.
<dt><b>program_date_time</b>
<dd>Generate <tt>&quot;EXT-X-PROGRAM-DATE-TIME&quot;</tt> tags.
<dt><b>second_level_segment_index</b>
<dd>Makes it possible to use segment indexes as %%d in hls_segment_filename expression besides date/time values when use_localtime is on. To get fixed width numbers with trailing zeroes, %%0xd format is available where x is the required width.
<dt><b>second_level_segment_size</b>
<dd>Makes it possible to use segment sizes (counted in bytes) as %%s in hls_segment_filename expression besides date/time values when use_localtime is on. To get fixed width numbers with trailing zeroes, %%0xs format is available where x is the required width.
<dt><b>second_level_segment_duration</b>
<dd>Makes it possible to use segment duration (calculated in microseconds) as %%t in hls_segment_filename expression besides date/time values when use_localtime is on. To get fixed width numbers with trailing zeroes, %%0xt format is available where x is the required width. 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i sample.mpeg \
 -f hls -hls_time 3 -hls_list_size 5 \
 -hls_flags second_level_segment_index+second_level_segment_size+second_level_segment_duration \
 -use_localtime 1 -use_localtime_mkdir 1 -hls_segment_filename &quot;segment_%Y%m%d%H%M%S_%%04d_%%08s_%%013t.ts&quot; stream.m3u8</pre>This will produce segments like this: <i>segment_20170102194334_0003_00122200_0000003000000.ts</i>, <i>segment_20170102194334_0004_00120072_0000003000000.ts</i> etc.
<dt><b>temp_file</b>
<dd>Write segment data to filename.tmp and rename to filename only once the segment is complete. A webserver serving up segments can be configured to reject requests to *.tmp to prevent access to in-progress segments before they have been added to the m3u8 playlist.</dl></dl><dl COMPACT><dd></dl><dt><b>hls_playlist_type event</b>
<dd>Emit <tt>&quot;#EXT-X-PLAYLIST-TYPE:EVENT&quot;</tt> in the m3u8 header. Forces <b>hls_list_size</b> to 0; the playlist can only be appended to.
<dt><b>hls_playlist_type vod</b>
<dd>Emit <tt>&quot;#EXT-X-PLAYLIST-TYPE:VOD&quot;</tt> in the m3u8 header. Forces <b>hls_list_size</b> to 0; the playlist must not change.
<dt><b>method</b>
<dd>Use the given <font SIZE="-1">HTTP</font> method to create the hls files. 

 <pre> ffmpeg -re -i in.ts -f hls -method PUT <a rel="nofollow" HREF="http://example.com/live/out.m3u8">http://example.com/live/out.m3u8</a></pre>This example will upload all the mpegts segment files to the <font SIZE="-1">HTTP</font> server using the <font SIZE="-1">HTTP PUT</font> method, and update the m3u8 files every <tt>&quot;refresh&quot;</tt> times using the same method. Note that the <font SIZE="-1">HTTP</font> server must support the given method for uploading files.
<dt><b>http_user_agent</b>
<dd>Override User-Agent field in <font SIZE="-1">HTTP</font> header. Applicable only for <font SIZE="-1">HTTP</font> output.</dl><h3>ico</h3><font SIZE="-1">ICO</font> file muxer. 

 Microsoft's icon file format (<font SIZE="-1">ICO</font>) has some strict limitations that should be noted:
<dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>Size cannot exceed 256 pixels in any dimension
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Only <font SIZE="-1">BMP</font> and <font SIZE="-1">PNG</font> images can be stored
<dt>&bull;
<dd>If a <font SIZE="-1">BMP</font> image is used, it must be one of the following pixel formats: 

 <pre> BMP Bit Depth FFmpeg Pixel Format
 1bit pal8
 4bit pal8
 8bit pal8
 16bit rgb555le
 24bit bgr24
 32bit bgra</pre><dt>&bull;
<dd>If a <font SIZE="-1">BMP</font> image is used, it must use the <font SIZE="-1">BITMAPINFOHEADER DIB</font> header
<dt>&bull;
<dd>If a <font SIZE="-1">PNG</font> image is used, it must use the rgba pixel format</dl><h3>image2</h3>Image file muxer. 

 The image file muxer writes video frames to image files. 

 The output filenames are specified by a pattern, which can be used to produce sequentially numbered series of files. The pattern may contain the string ``%d'' or &quot;%0<i>N</i>d``, this string specifies the position of the characters representing a numbering in the filenames. If the form ''%0<i>N</i>d&quot; is used, the string representing the number in each filename is 0-padded to <i>N</i> digits. The literal character '%' can be specified in the pattern with the string ``%%''. 

 If the pattern contains ``%d'' or &quot;%0<i>N</i>d&quot;, the first filename of the file list specified will contain the number 1, all the following numbers will be sequential. 

 The pattern may contain a suffix which is used to automatically determine the format of the image files to write. 

 For example the pattern ``img-%03d.bmp'' will specify a sequence of filenames of the form <i>img-001.bmp</i>, <i>img-002.bmp</i>, ..., <i>img-010.bmp</i>, etc. The pattern ``img%%-%d.jpg'' will specify a sequence of filenames of the form <i>img%-1.jpg</i>, <i>img%-2.jpg</i>, ..., <i>img%-10.jpg</i>, etc. 

 <i>Examples</i> 

 The following example shows how to use <b>ffmpeg</b> for creating a sequence of files <i>img-001.jpeg</i>, <i>img-002.jpeg</i>, ..., taking one image every second from the input video: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i in.avi -vsync cfr -r 1 -f image2 'img-%03d.jpeg'</pre>Note that with <b>ffmpeg</b>, if the format is not specified with the <tt>&quot;-f&quot;</tt> option and the output filename specifies an image file format, the image2 muxer is automatically selected, so the previous command can be written as: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i in.avi -vsync cfr -r 1 'img-%03d.jpeg'</pre>Note also that the pattern must not necessarily contain ``%d'' or &quot;%0<i>N</i>d&quot;, for example to create a single image file <i>img.jpeg</i> from the start of the input video you can employ the command: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i in.avi -f image2 -frames:v 1 img.jpeg</pre>The <b>strftime</b> option allows you to expand the filename with date and time information. Check the documentation of the <tt>&quot;strftime()&quot;</tt> function for the syntax. 

 For example to generate image files from the <tt>&quot;strftime()&quot;</tt> ``%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S'' pattern, the following <b>ffmpeg</b> command can be used: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -f v4l2 -r 1 -i /dev/video0 -f image2 -strftime 1 &quot;%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S.jpg&quot;</pre><i>Options</i>
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>start_number</b>
<dd>Start the sequence from the specified number. Default value is 1.
<dt><b>update</b>
<dd>If set to 1, the filename will always be interpreted as just a filename, not a pattern, and the corresponding file will be continuously overwritten with new images. Default value is 0.
<dt><b>strftime</b>
<dd>If set to 1, expand the filename with date and time information from <tt>&quot;strftime()&quot;</tt>. Default value is 0.</dl>
 

 The image muxer supports the .Y.U.V image file format. This format is special in that that each image frame consists of three files, for each of the <font SIZE="-1">YUV420P</font> components. To read or write this image file format, specify the name of the '.Y' file. The muxer will automatically open the '.U' and '.V' files as required.
<h3>matroska</h3>Matroska container muxer. 

 This muxer implements the matroska and webm container specs. 

 <i>Metadata</i> 

 The recognized metadata settings in this muxer are:
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>title</b>
<dd>Set title name provided to a single track.
<dt><b>language</b>
<dd>Specify the language of the track in the Matroska languages form. 

 The language can be either the 3 letters bibliographic <font SIZE="-1">ISO-639-2</font> (<font SIZE="-1">ISO 639-2/B</font>) form (like ``fre'' for French), or a language code mixed with a country code for specialities in languages (like ``fre-ca'' for Canadian French).
<dt><b>stereo_mode</b>
<dd>Set stereo 3D video layout of two views in a single video track. 

 The following values are recognized:
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt><b>mono</b>
<dd>video is not stereo
<dt><b>left_right</b>
<dd>Both views are arranged side by side, Left-eye view is on the left
<dt><b>bottom_top</b>
<dd>Both views are arranged in top-bottom orientation, Left-eye view is at bottom
<dt><b>top_bottom</b>
<dd>Both views are arranged in top-bottom orientation, Left-eye view is on top
<dt><b>checkerboard_rl</b>
<dd>Each view is arranged in a checkerboard interleaved pattern, Left-eye view being first
<dt><b>checkerboard_lr</b>
<dd>Each view is arranged in a checkerboard interleaved pattern, Right-eye view being first
<dt><b>row_interleaved_rl</b>
<dd>Each view is constituted by a row based interleaving, Right-eye view is first row
<dt><b>row_interleaved_lr</b>
<dd>Each view is constituted by a row based interleaving, Left-eye view is first row
<dt><b>col_interleaved_rl</b>
<dd>Both views are arranged in a column based interleaving manner, Right-eye view is first column
<dt><b>col_interleaved_lr</b>
<dd>Both views are arranged in a column based interleaving manner, Left-eye view is first column
<dt><b>anaglyph_cyan_red</b>
<dd>All frames are in anaglyph format viewable through red-cyan filters
<dt><b>right_left</b>
<dd>Both views are arranged side by side, Right-eye view is on the left
<dt><b>anaglyph_green_magenta</b>
<dd>All frames are in anaglyph format viewable through green-magenta filters
<dt><b>block_lr</b>
<dd>Both eyes laced in one Block, Left-eye view is first
<dt><b>block_rl</b>
<dd>Both eyes laced in one Block, Right-eye view is first</dl></dl><dl COMPACT><dd></dl></dl>
 

 For example a 3D WebM clip can be created using the following command line: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i sample_left_right_clip.mpg -an -c:v libvpx -metadata stereo_mode=left_right -y stereo_clip.webm</pre><i>Options</i> 

 This muxer supports the following options:
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>reserve_index_space</b>
<dd>By default, this muxer writes the index for seeking (called cues in Matroska terms) at the end of the file, because it cannot know in advance how much space to leave for the index at the beginning of the file. However for some use cases --- e.g. streaming where seeking is possible but slow --- it is useful to put the index at the beginning of the file. 

 If this option is set to a non-zero value, the muxer will reserve a given amount of space in the file header and then try to write the cues there when the muxing finishes. If the available space does not suffice, muxing will fail. A safe size for most use cases should be about 50kB per hour of video. 

 Note that cues are only written if the output is seekable and this option will have no effect if it is not.</dl><h3>md5</h3><font SIZE="-1">MD5</font> testing format. 

 This is a variant of the <b>hash</b> muxer. Unlike that muxer, it defaults to using the <font SIZE="-1">MD5</font> hash function. 

 <i>Examples</i> 

 To compute the <font SIZE="-1">MD5</font> hash of the input converted to raw audio and video, and store it in the file <i>out.md5</i>: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i INPUT -f md5 out.md5</pre>You can print the <font SIZE="-1">MD5</font> to stdout with the command: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i INPUT -f md5 -</pre>See also the <b>hash</b> and <b>framemd5</b> muxers.
<h3>mov, mp4, ismv</h3><font SIZE="-1">MOV/MP4/ISMV</font> (Smooth Streaming) muxer. 

 The mov/mp4/ismv muxer supports fragmentation. Normally, a <font SIZE="-1">MOV/MP4</font> file has all the metadata about all packets stored in one location (written at the end of the file, it can be moved to the start for better playback by adding <i>faststart</i> to the <i>movflags</i>, or using the <b>qt-faststart</b> tool). A fragmented file consists of a number of fragments, where packets and metadata about these packets are stored together. Writing a fragmented file has the advantage that the file is decodable even if the writing is interrupted (while a normal <font SIZE="-1">MOV/MP4</font> is undecodable if it is not properly finished), and it requires less memory when writing very long files (since writing normal <font SIZE="-1">MOV/MP4</font> files stores info about every single packet in memory until the file is closed). The downside is that it is less compatible with other applications. 

 <i>Options</i> 

 Fragmentation is enabled by setting one of the AVOptions that define how to cut the file into fragments:
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>-moov_size</b> <i>bytes</i>
<dd>Reserves space for the moov atom at the beginning of the file instead of placing the moov atom at the end. If the space reserved is insufficient, muxing will fail.
<dt><b>-movflags frag_keyframe</b>
<dd>Start a new fragment at each video keyframe.
<dt><b>-frag_duration</b> <i>duration</i>
<dd>Create fragments that are <i>duration</i> microseconds long.
<dt><b>-frag_size</b> <i>size</i>
<dd>Create fragments that contain up to <i>size</i> bytes of payload data.
<dt><b>-movflags frag_custom</b>
<dd>Allow the caller to manually choose when to cut fragments, by calling <tt>&quot;av_write_frame(ctx, NULL)&quot;</tt> to write a fragment with the packets written so far. (This is only useful with other applications integrating libavformat, not from <b>ffmpeg</b>.)
<dt><b>-min_frag_duration</b> <i>duration</i>
<dd>Don't create fragments that are shorter than <i>duration</i> microseconds long.</dl>
 

 If more than one condition is specified, fragments are cut when one of the specified conditions is fulfilled. The exception to this is <tt>&quot;-min_frag_duration&quot;</tt>, which has to be fulfilled for any of the other conditions to apply. 

 Additionally, the way the output file is written can be adjusted through a few other options:
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>-movflags empty_moov</b>
<dd>Write an initial moov atom directly at the start of the file, without describing any samples in it. Generally, an mdat/moov pair is written at the start of the file, as a normal <font SIZE="-1">MOV/MP4</font> file, containing only a short portion of the file. With this option set, there is no initial mdat atom, and the moov atom only describes the tracks but has a zero duration. 

 This option is implicitly set when writing ismv (Smooth Streaming) files.
<dt><b>-movflags separate_moof</b>
<dd>Write a separate moof (movie fragment) atom for each track. Normally, packets for all tracks are written in a moof atom (which is slightly more efficient), but with this option set, the muxer writes one moof/mdat pair for each track, making it easier to separate tracks. 

 This option is implicitly set when writing ismv (Smooth Streaming) files.
<dt><b>-movflags faststart</b>
<dd>Run a second pass moving the index (moov atom) to the beginning of the file. This operation can take a while, and will not work in various situations such as fragmented output, thus it is not enabled by default.
<dt><b>-movflags rtphint</b>
<dd>Add <font SIZE="-1">RTP</font> hinting tracks to the output file.
<dt><b>-movflags disable_chpl</b>
<dd>Disable Nero chapter markers (chpl atom). Normally, both Nero chapters and a QuickTime chapter track are written to the file. With this option set, only the QuickTime chapter track will be written. Nero chapters can cause failures when the file is reprocessed with certain tagging programs, like mp3Tag 2.61a and iTunes 11.3, most likely other versions are affected as well.
<dt><b>-movflags omit_tfhd_offset</b>
<dd>Do not write any absolute base_data_offset in tfhd atoms. This avoids tying fragments to absolute byte positions in the file/streams.
<dt><b>-movflags default_base_moof</b>
<dd>Similarly to the omit_tfhd_offset, this flag avoids writing the absolute base_data_offset field in tfhd atoms, but does so by using the new default-base-is-moof flag instead. This flag is new from 14496-12:2012. This may make the fragments easier to parse in certain circumstances (avoiding basing track fragment location calculations on the implicit end of the previous track fragment).
<dt><b>-write_tmcd</b>
<dd>Specify <tt>&quot;on&quot;</tt> to force writing a timecode track, <tt>&quot;off&quot;</tt> to disable it and <tt>&quot;auto&quot;</tt> to write a timecode track only for mov and mp4 output (default).
<dt><b>-movflags negative_cts_offsets</b>
<dd>Enables utilization of version 1 of the <font SIZE="-1">CTTS</font> box, in which the <font SIZE="-1">CTS</font> offsets can be negative. This enables the initial sample to have <font SIZE="-1">DTS/CTS</font> of zero, and reduces the need for edit lists for some cases such as video tracks with B-frames. Additionally, eases conformance with the DASH-IF interoperability guidelines.</dl>
 

 <i>Example</i> 

 Smooth Streaming content can be pushed in real time to a publishing point on <font SIZE="-1">IIS</font> with this muxer. Example: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -re &lt;&lt;normal input/transcoding options&gt;&gt; -movflags isml+frag_keyframe -f ismv <a rel="nofollow" HREF="http://server/publishingpoint.isml/Streams(Encoder1)">http://server/publishingpoint.isml/Streams(Encoder1)</a></pre><i>Audible </i><font SIZE="-1"><i>AAX</i></font><i></i> 

 Audible <font SIZE="-1">AAX</font> files are encrypted M4B files, and they can be decrypted by specifying a 4 byte activation secret. 

 <pre> ffmpeg -activation_bytes 1CEB00DA -i test.aax -vn -c:a copy output.mp4</pre><h3>mp3</h3>The <font SIZE="-1">MP3</font> muxer writes a raw <font SIZE="-1">MP3</font> stream with the following optional features:
<dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>An ID3v2 metadata header at the beginning (enabled by default). Versions 2.3 and 2.4 are supported, the <tt>&quot;id3v2_version&quot;</tt> private option controls which one is used (3 or 4). Setting <tt>&quot;id3v2_version&quot;</tt> to 0 disables the ID3v2 header completely. 

 The muxer supports writing attached pictures (<font SIZE="-1">APIC</font> frames) to the ID3v2 header. The pictures are supplied to the muxer in form of a video stream with a single packet. There can be any number of those streams, each will correspond to a single <font SIZE="-1">APIC</font> frame. The stream metadata tags <i>title</i> and <i>comment</i> map to <font SIZE="-1">APIC</font> <i>description</i> and <i>picture type</i> respectively. See &lt;<b><a rel="nofollow" HREF="http://id3.org/id3v2.4.0-frames">http://id3.org/id3v2.4.0-frames</a></b>&gt; for allowed picture types. 

 Note that the <font SIZE="-1">APIC</font> frames must be written at the beginning, so the muxer will buffer the audio frames until it gets all the pictures. It is therefore advised to provide the pictures as soon as possible to avoid excessive buffering.
<dt>&bull;
<dd>A Xing/LAME frame right after the ID3v2 header (if present). It is enabled by default, but will be written only if the output is seekable. The <tt>&quot;write_xing&quot;</tt> private option can be used to disable it. The frame contains various information that may be useful to the decoder, like the audio duration or encoder delay.
<dt>&bull;
<dd>A legacy ID3v1 tag at the end of the file (disabled by default). It may be enabled with the <tt>&quot;write_id3v1&quot;</tt> private option, but as its capabilities are very limited, its usage is not recommended.</dl>
 

 Examples: 

 Write an mp3 with an ID3v2.3 header and an ID3v1 footer: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i INPUT -id3v2_version 3 -write_id3v1 1 out.mp3</pre>To attach a picture to an mp3 file select both the audio and the picture stream with <tt>&quot;map&quot;</tt>: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i input.mp3 -i cover.png -c copy -map 0 -map 1
 -metadata:s:v title=&quot;Album cover&quot; -metadata:s:v comment=&quot;Cover (Front)&quot; out.mp3</pre>Write a ``clean'' <font SIZE="-1">MP3</font> without any extra features: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i input.wav -write_xing 0 -id3v2_version 0 out.mp3</pre><h3>mpegts</h3><font SIZE="-1">MPEG</font> transport stream muxer. 

 This muxer implements <font SIZE="-1">ISO 13818-1</font> and part of <font SIZE="-1">ETSI EN 300 468.</font> 

 The recognized metadata settings in mpegts muxer are <tt>&quot;service_provider&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;service_name&quot;</tt>. If they are not set the default for <tt>&quot;service_provider&quot;</tt> is <b>FFmpeg</b> and the default for <tt>&quot;service_name&quot;</tt> is <b>Service01</b>. 

 <i>Options</i> 

 The muxer options are:
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>mpegts_transport_stream_id</b> <i>integer</i>
<dd>Set the <b>transport_stream_id</b>. This identifies a transponder in <font SIZE="-1">DVB.</font> Default is <tt>0x0001</tt>.
<dt><b>mpegts_original_network_id</b> <i>integer</i>
<dd>Set the <b>original_network_id</b>. This is unique identifier of a network in <font SIZE="-1">DVB.</font> Its main use is in the unique identification of a service through the path <b>Original_Network_ID, Transport_Stream_ID</b>. Default is <tt>0x0001</tt>.
<dt><b>mpegts_service_id</b> <i>integer</i>
<dd>Set the <b>service_id</b>, also known as program in <font SIZE="-1">DVB.</font> Default is <tt>0x0001</tt>.
<dt><b>mpegts_service_type</b> <i>integer</i>
<dd>Set the program <b>service_type</b>. Default is <tt>&quot;digital_tv&quot;</tt>. Accepts the following options:
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt><b>hex_value</b>
<dd>Any hexdecimal value between <tt>0x01</tt> to <tt>0xff</tt> as defined in <font SIZE="-1">ETSI 300 468.</font>
<dt><b>digital_tv</b>
<dd>Digital <font SIZE="-1">TV</font> service.
<dt><b>digital_radio</b>
<dd>Digital Radio service.
<dt><b>teletext</b>
<dd>Teletext service.
<dt><b>advanced_codec_digital_radio</b>
<dd>Advanced Codec Digital Radio service.
<dt><b>mpeg2_digital_hdtv</b>
<dd><font SIZE="-1">MPEG2</font> Digital <font SIZE="-1">HDTV</font> service.
<dt><b>advanced_codec_digital_sdtv</b>
<dd>Advanced Codec Digital <font SIZE="-1">SDTV</font> service.
<dt><b>advanced_codec_digital_hdtv</b>
<dd>Advanced Codec Digital <font SIZE="-1">HDTV</font> service.</dl></dl><dl COMPACT><dd></dl><dt><b>mpegts_pmt_start_pid</b> <i>integer</i>
<dd>Set the first <font SIZE="-1">PID</font> for <font SIZE="-1">PMT.</font> Default is <tt>0x1000</tt>. Max is <tt>0x1f00</tt>.
<dt><b>mpegts_start_pid</b> <i>integer</i>
<dd>Set the first <font SIZE="-1">PID</font> for data packets. Default is <tt>0x0100</tt>. Max is <tt>0x0f00</tt>.
<dt><b>mpegts_m2ts_mode</b> <i>boolean</i>
<dd>Enable m2ts mode if set to <tt>1</tt>. Default value is <tt>&quot;-1&quot;</tt> which disables m2ts mode.
<dt><b>muxrate</b> <i>integer</i>
<dd>Set a constant muxrate. Default is <font SIZE="-1">VBR.</font>
<dt><b>pes_payload_size</b> <i>integer</i>
<dd>Set minimum <font SIZE="-1">PES</font> packet payload in bytes. Default is <tt>2930</tt>.
<dt><b>mpegts_flags</b> <i>flags</i>
<dd>Set mpegts flags. Accepts the following options:
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt><b>resend_headers</b>
<dd>Reemit <font SIZE="-1">PAT/PMT</font> before writing the next packet.
<dt><b>latm</b>
<dd>Use <font SIZE="-1">LATM</font> packetization for <font SIZE="-1">AAC.</font>
<dt><b>pat_pmt_at_frames</b>
<dd>Reemit <font SIZE="-1">PAT</font> and <font SIZE="-1">PMT</font> at each video frame.
<dt><b>system_b</b>
<dd>Conform to System B (<font SIZE="-1">DVB</font>) instead of System A (<font SIZE="-1">ATSC</font>).
<dt><b>initial_discontinuity</b>
<dd>Mark the initial packet of each stream as discontinuity.</dl></dl><dl COMPACT><dd></dl><dt><b>resend_headers</b> <i>integer</i>
<dd>Reemit <font SIZE="-1">PAT/PMT</font> before writing the next packet. This option is deprecated: use <b>mpegts_flags</b> instead.
<dt><b>mpegts_copyts</b> <i>boolean</i>
<dd>Preserve original timestamps, if value is set to <tt>1</tt>. Default value is <tt>&quot;-1&quot;</tt>, which results in shifting timestamps so that they start from 0.
<dt><b>omit_video_pes_length</b> <i>boolean</i>
<dd>Omit the <font SIZE="-1">PES</font> packet length for video packets. Default is <tt>1</tt> (true).
<dt><b>pcr_period</b> <i>integer</i>
<dd>Override the default <font SIZE="-1">PCR</font> retransmission time in milliseconds. Ignored if variable muxrate is selected. Default is <tt>20</tt>.
<dt><b>pat_period</b> <i>double</i>
<dd>Maximum time in seconds between <font SIZE="-1">PAT/PMT</font> tables.
<dt><b>sdt_period</b> <i>double</i>
<dd>Maximum time in seconds between <font SIZE="-1">SDT</font> tables.
<dt><b>tables_version</b> <i>integer</i>
<dd>Set <font SIZE="-1">PAT, PMT</font> and <font SIZE="-1">SDT</font> version (default <tt>0</tt>, valid values are from 0 to 31, inclusively). This option allows updating stream structure so that standard consumer may detect the change. To do so, reopen output <tt>&quot;AVFormatContext&quot;</tt> (in case of <font SIZE="-1">API</font> usage) or restart <b>ffmpeg</b> instance, cyclically changing <b>tables_version</b> value: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i source1.ts -codec copy -f mpegts -tables_version 0 <a HREF="udp://1.1.1.1:1111">udp://1.1.1.1:1111</a>
 ffmpeg -i source2.ts -codec copy -f mpegts -tables_version 1 <a HREF="udp://1.1.1.1:1111">udp://1.1.1.1:1111</a>
 ...
 ffmpeg -i source3.ts -codec copy -f mpegts -tables_version 31 <a HREF="udp://1.1.1.1:1111">udp://1.1.1.1:1111</a>
 ffmpeg -i source1.ts -codec copy -f mpegts -tables_version 0 <a HREF="udp://1.1.1.1:1111">udp://1.1.1.1:1111</a>
 ffmpeg -i source2.ts -codec copy -f mpegts -tables_version 1 <a HREF="udp://1.1.1.1:1111">udp://1.1.1.1:1111</a>
 ...</pre></dl>
 

 <i>Example</i> 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i file.mpg -c copy \
 -mpegts_original_network_id 0x1122 \
 -mpegts_transport_stream_id 0x3344 \
 -mpegts_service_id 0x5566 \
 -mpegts_pmt_start_pid 0x1500 \
 -mpegts_start_pid 0x150 \
 -metadata service_provider=&quot;Some provider&quot; \
 -metadata service_name=&quot;Some Channel&quot; \
 out.ts</pre><h3>mxf, mxf_d10</h3><font SIZE="-1">MXF</font> muxer. 

 <i>Options</i> 

 The muxer options are:
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>store_user_comments</b> <i>bool</i>
<dd>Set if user comments should be stored if available or never. <font SIZE="-1">IRT D-10</font> does not allow user comments. The default is thus to write them for mxf but not for mxf_d10</dl><h3>null</h3>Null muxer. 

 This muxer does not generate any output file, it is mainly useful for testing or benchmarking purposes. 

 For example to benchmark decoding with <b>ffmpeg</b> you can use the command: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -benchmark -i INPUT -f null out.null</pre>Note that the above command does not read or write the <i>out.null</i> file, but specifying the output file is required by the <b>ffmpeg</b> syntax. 

 Alternatively you can write the command as: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -benchmark -i INPUT -f null -</pre><h3>nut</h3><dl COMPACT><dt><b>-syncpoints</b> <i>flags</i>
<dd>Change the syncpoint usage in nut:
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt><i>default</i> <b>use the normal low-overhead seeking aids.</b>
<dd><dt><i>none</i> <b>do not use the syncpoints at all, reducing the overhead but making the stream non-seekable;</b>
<dd><pre> Use of this option is not recommended, as the resulting files are very damage
 sensitive and seeking is not possible. Also in general the overhead from
 syncpoints is negligible. Note, -C&lt;write_index&gt; 0 can be used to disable
 all growing data tables, allowing to mux endless streams with limited memory
 and without these disadvantages.</pre><dt><i>timestamped</i> <b>extend the syncpoint with a wallclock field.</b>
<dd></dl></dl><dl COMPACT><dd>The <i>none</i> and <i>timestamped</i> flags are experimental.</dl><dt><b>-write_index</b> <i>bool</i>
<dd>Write index at the end, the default is to write an index.</dl>
 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i INPUT -f_strict experimental -syncpoints none - | processor</pre><h3>ogg</h3>Ogg container muxer.
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>-page_duration</b> <i>duration</i>
<dd>Preferred page duration, in microseconds. The muxer will attempt to create pages that are approximately <i>duration</i> microseconds long. This allows the user to compromise between seek granularity and container overhead. The default is 1 second. A value of 0 will fill all segments, making pages as large as possible. A value of 1 will effectively use 1 packet-per-page in most situations, giving a small seek granularity at the cost of additional container overhead.
<dt><b>-serial_offset</b> <i>value</i>
<dd>Serial value from which to set the streams serial number. Setting it to different and sufficiently large values ensures that the produced ogg files can be safely chained.</dl><h3>segment, stream_segment, ssegment</h3>Basic stream segmenter. 

 This muxer outputs streams to a number of separate files of nearly fixed duration. Output filename pattern can be set in a fashion similar to <b>image2</b>, or by using a <tt>&quot;strftime&quot;</tt> template if the <b>strftime</b> option is enabled. 

 <tt>&quot;stream_segment&quot;</tt> is a variant of the muxer used to write to streaming output formats, i.e. which do not require global headers, and is recommended for outputting e.g. to <font SIZE="-1">MPEG</font> transport stream segments. <tt>&quot;ssegment&quot;</tt> is a shorter alias for <tt>&quot;stream_segment&quot;</tt>. 

 Every segment starts with a keyframe of the selected reference stream, which is set through the <b>reference_stream</b> option. 

 Note that if you want accurate splitting for a video file, you need to make the input key frames correspond to the exact splitting times expected by the segmenter, or the segment muxer will start the new segment with the key frame found next after the specified start time. 

 The segment muxer works best with a single constant frame rate video. 

 Optionally it can generate a list of the created segments, by setting the option <i>segment_list</i>. The list type is specified by the <i>segment_list_type</i> option. The entry filenames in the segment list are set by default to the basename of the corresponding segment files. 

 See also the <b>hls</b> muxer, which provides a more specific implementation for <font SIZE="-1">HLS</font> segmentation. 

 <i>Options</i> 

 The segment muxer supports the following options:
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>increment_tc</b> <i>1|0</i>
<dd>if set to <tt>1</tt>, increment timecode between each segment If this is selected, the input need to have a timecode in the first video stream. Default value is <tt>0</tt>.
<dt><b>reference_stream</b> <i>specifier</i>
<dd>Set the reference stream, as specified by the string <i>specifier</i>. If <i>specifier</i> is set to <tt>&quot;auto&quot;</tt>, the reference is chosen automatically. Otherwise it must be a stream specifier (see the ``Stream specifiers'' chapter in the ffmpeg manual) which specifies the reference stream. The default value is <tt>&quot;auto&quot;</tt>.
<dt><b>segment_format</b> <i>format</i>
<dd>Override the inner container format, by default it is guessed by the filename extension.
<dt><b>segment_format_options</b> <i>options_list</i>
<dd>Set output format options using a :-separated list of key=value parameters. Values containing the <tt>&quot;:&quot;</tt> special character must be escaped.
<dt><b>segment_list</b> <i>name</i>
<dd>Generate also a listfile named <i>name</i>. If not specified no listfile is generated.
<dt><b>segment_list_flags</b> <i>flags</i>
<dd>Set flags affecting the segment list generation. 

 It currently supports the following flags:
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt><b>cache</b>
<dd>Allow caching (only affects M3U8 list files).
<dt><b>live</b>
<dd>Allow live-friendly file generation.</dl></dl><dl COMPACT><dd></dl><dt><b>segment_list_size</b> <i>size</i>
<dd>Update the list file so that it contains at most <i>size</i> segments. If 0 the list file will contain all the segments. Default value is 0.
<dt><b>segment_list_entry_prefix</b> <i>prefix</i>
<dd>Prepend <i>prefix</i> to each entry. Useful to generate absolute paths. By default no prefix is applied.
<dt><b>segment_list_type</b> <i>type</i>
<dd>Select the listing format. 

 The following values are recognized:
<dl COMPACT><dd><dl COMPACT><dt><b>flat</b>
<dd>Generate a flat list for the created segments, one segment per line.
<dt><b>csv, ext</b>
<dd>Generate a list for the created segments, one segment per line, each line matching the format (comma-separated values): 

 <pre> &lt;segment_filename&gt;,&lt;segment_start_time&gt;,&lt;segment_end_time&gt;</pre><i>segment_filename</i> is the name of the output file generated by the muxer according to the provided pattern. <font SIZE="-1">CSV</font> escaping (according to <font SIZE="-1">RFC4180</font>) is applied if required. 

 <i>segment_start_time</i> and <i>segment_end_time</i> specify the segment start and end time expressed in seconds. 

 A list file with the suffix <tt>&quot;.csv&quot;</tt> or <tt>&quot;.ext&quot;</tt> will auto-select this format. 

 <b>ext</b> is deprecated in favor or <b>csv</b>.
<dt><b>ffconcat</b>
<dd>Generate an ffconcat file for the created segments. The resulting file can be read using the FFmpeg <b>concat</b> demuxer. 

 A list file with the suffix <tt>&quot;.ffcat&quot;</tt> or <tt>&quot;.ffconcat&quot;</tt> will auto-select this format.
<dt><b>m3u8</b>
<dd>Generate an extended M3U8 file, version 3, compliant with &lt;<b><a rel="nofollow" HREF="http://tools.ietf.org/id/draft-pantos-http-live-streaming">http://tools.ietf.org/id/draft-pantos-http-live-streaming</a></b>&gt;. 

 A list file with the suffix <tt>&quot;.m3u8&quot;</tt> will auto-select this format.</dl></dl><dl COMPACT><dd>If not specified the type is guessed from the list file name suffix.</dl><dt><b>segment_time</b> <i>time</i>
<dd>Set segment duration to <i>time</i>, the value must be a duration specification. Default value is ``2''. See also the <b>segment_times</b> option. 

 Note that splitting may not be accurate, unless you force the reference stream key-frames at the given time. See the introductory notice and the examples below.
<dt><b>segment_atclocktime</b> <i>1|0</i>
<dd>If set to ``1'' split at regular clock time intervals starting from 00:00 o'clock. The <i>time</i> value specified in <b>segment_time</b> is used for setting the length of the splitting interval. 

 For example with <b>segment_time</b> set to ``900'' this makes it possible to create files at 12:00 o'clock, 12:15, 12:30, etc. 

 Default value is ``0''.
<dt><b>segment_clocktime_offset</b> <i>duration</i>
<dd>Delay the segment splitting times with the specified duration when using <b>segment_atclocktime</b>. 

 For example with <b>segment_time</b> set to ``900'' and <b>segment_clocktime_offset</b> set to ``300'' this makes it possible to create files at 12:05, 12:20, 12:35, etc. 

 Default value is ``0''.
<dt><b>segment_clocktime_wrap_duration</b> <i>duration</i>
<dd>Force the segmenter to only start a new segment if a packet reaches the muxer within the specified duration after the segmenting clock time. This way you can make the segmenter more resilient to backward local time jumps, such as leap seconds or transition to standard time from daylight savings time. 

 Default is the maximum possible duration which means starting a new segment regardless of the elapsed time since the last clock time.
<dt><b>segment_time_delta</b> <i>delta</i>
<dd>Specify the accuracy time when selecting the start time for a segment, expressed as a duration specification. Default value is ``0''. 

 When delta is specified a key-frame will start a new segment if its <font SIZE="-1">PTS</font> satisfies the relation: 

 <pre> PTS &gt;= start_time - time_delta</pre>This option is useful when splitting video content, which is always split at <font SIZE="-1">GOP</font> boundaries, in case a key frame is found just before the specified split time. 

 In particular may be used in combination with the <i>ffmpeg</i> option <i>force_key_frames</i>. The key frame times specified by <i>force_key_frames</i> may not be set accurately because of rounding issues, with the consequence that a key frame time may result set just before the specified time. For constant frame rate videos a value of 1/(2*<i>frame_rate</i>) should address the worst case mismatch between the specified time and the time set by <i>force_key_frames</i>.
<dt><b>segment_times</b> <i>times</i>
<dd>Specify a list of split points. <i>times</i> contains a list of comma separated duration specifications, in increasing order. See also the <b>segment_time</b> option.
<dt><b>segment_frames</b> <i>frames</i>
<dd>Specify a list of split video frame numbers. <i>frames</i> contains a list of comma separated integer numbers, in increasing order. 

 This option specifies to start a new segment whenever a reference stream key frame is found and the sequential number (starting from 0) of the frame is greater or equal to the next value in the list.
<dt><b>segment_wrap</b> <i>limit</i>
<dd>Wrap around segment index once it reaches <i>limit</i>.
<dt><b>segment_start_number</b> <i>number</i>
<dd>Set the sequence number of the first segment. Defaults to <tt>0</tt>.
<dt><b>strftime</b> <i>1|0</i>
<dd>Use the <tt>&quot;strftime&quot;</tt> function to define the name of the new segments to write. If this is selected, the output segment name must contain a <tt>&quot;strftime&quot;</tt> function template. Default value is <tt>0</tt>.
<dt><b>break_non_keyframes</b> <i>1|0</i>
<dd>If enabled, allow segments to start on frames other than keyframes. This improves behavior on some players when the time between keyframes is inconsistent, but may make things worse on others, and can cause some oddities during seeking. Defaults to <tt>0</tt>.
<dt><b>reset_timestamps</b> <i>1|0</i>
<dd>Reset timestamps at the beginning of each segment, so that each segment will start with near-zero timestamps. It is meant to ease the playback of the generated segments. May not work with some combinations of muxers/codecs. It is set to <tt>0</tt> by default.
<dt><b>initial_offset</b> <i>offset</i>
<dd>Specify timestamp offset to apply to the output packet timestamps. The argument must be a time duration specification, and defaults to 0.
<dt><b>write_empty_segments</b> <i>1|0</i>
<dd>If enabled, write an empty segment if there are no packets during the period a segment would usually span. Otherwise, the segment will be filled with the next packet written. Defaults to <tt>0</tt>.</dl>
 

 <i>Examples</i>
<dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>Remux the content of file <i>in.mkv</i> to a list of segments <i>out-000.nut</i>, <i>out-001.nut</i>, etc., and write the list of generated segments to <i>out.list</i>: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i in.mkv -codec copy -map 0 -f segment -segment_list out.list out%03d.nut</pre><dt>&bull;
<dd>Segment input and set output format options for the output segments: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i in.mkv -f segment -segment_time 10 -segment_format_options movflags=+faststart out%03d.mp4</pre><dt>&bull;
<dd>Segment the input file according to the split points specified by the <i>segment_times</i> option: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i in.mkv -codec copy -map 0 -f segment -segment_list out.csv -segment_times 1,2,3,5,8,13,21 out%03d.nut</pre><dt>&bull;
<dd>Use the <b>ffmpeg</b> <b>force_key_frames</b> option to force key frames in the input at the specified location, together with the segment option <b>segment_time_delta</b> to account for possible roundings operated when setting key frame times. 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i in.mkv -force_key_frames 1,2,3,5,8,13,21 -codec:v mpeg4 -codec:a pcm_s16le -map 0 \
 -f segment -segment_list out.csv -segment_times 1,2,3,5,8,13,21 -segment_time_delta 0.05 out%03d.nut</pre>In order to force key frames on the input file, transcoding is required.
<dt>&bull;
<dd>Segment the input file by splitting the input file according to the frame numbers sequence specified with the <b>segment_frames</b> option: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i in.mkv -codec copy -map 0 -f segment -segment_list out.csv -segment_frames 100,200,300,500,800 out%03d.nut</pre><dt>&bull;
<dd>Convert the <i>in.mkv</i> to <font SIZE="-1">TS</font> segments using the <tt>&quot;libx264&quot;</tt> and <tt>&quot;aac&quot;</tt> encoders: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i in.mkv -map 0 -codec:v libx264 -codec:a aac -f ssegment -segment_list out.list out%03d.ts</pre><dt>&bull;
<dd>Segment the input file, and create an M3U8 live playlist (can be used as live <font SIZE="-1">HLS</font> source): 

 <pre> ffmpeg -re -i in.mkv -codec copy -map 0 -f segment -segment_list playlist.m3u8 \
 -segment_list_flags +live -segment_time 10 out%03d.mkv</pre></dl><h3>smoothstreaming</h3>Smooth Streaming muxer generates a set of files (Manifest, chunks) suitable for serving with conventional web server.
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>window_size</b>
<dd>Specify the number of fragments kept in the manifest. Default 0 (keep all).
<dt><b>extra_window_size</b>
<dd>Specify the number of fragments kept outside of the manifest before removing from disk. Default 5.
<dt><b>lookahead_count</b>
<dd>Specify the number of lookahead fragments. Default 2.
<dt><b>min_frag_duration</b>
<dd>Specify the minimum fragment duration (in microseconds). Default 5000000.
<dt><b>remove_at_exit</b>
<dd>Specify whether to remove all fragments when finished. Default 0 (do not remove).</dl><h3>fifo</h3>The fifo pseudo-muxer allows the separation of encoding and muxing by using first-in-first-out queue and running the actual muxer in a separate thread. This is especially useful in combination with the <b>tee</b> muxer and can be used to send data to several destinations with different reliability/writing speed/latency. 

 <font SIZE="-1">API</font> users should be aware that callback functions (interrupt_callback, io_open and io_close) used within its AVFormatContext must be thread-safe. 

 The behavior of the fifo muxer if the queue fills up or if the output fails is selectable,
<dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>output can be transparently restarted with configurable delay between retries based on real time or time of the processed stream.
<dt>&bull;
<dd>encoding can be blocked during temporary failure, or continue transparently dropping packets in case fifo queue fills up.
<dt><b>fifo_format</b>
<dd>Specify the format name. Useful if it cannot be guessed from the output name suffix.
<dt><b>queue_size</b>
<dd>Specify size of the queue (number of packets). Default value is 60.
<dt><b>format_opts</b>
<dd>Specify format options for the underlying muxer. Muxer options can be specified as a list of <i>key</i>=<i>value</i> pairs separated by ':'.
<dt><b>drop_pkts_on_overflow</b> <i>bool</i>
<dd>If set to 1 (true), in case the fifo queue fills up, packets will be dropped rather than blocking the encoder. This makes it possible to continue streaming without delaying the input, at the cost of omitting part of the stream. By default this option is set to 0 (false), so in such cases the encoder will be blocked until the muxer processes some of the packets and none of them is lost.
<dt><b>attempt_recovery</b> <i>bool</i>
<dd>If failure occurs, attempt to recover the output. This is especially useful when used with network output, since it makes it possible to restart streaming transparently. By default this option is set to 0 (false).
<dt><b>max_recovery_attempts</b>
<dd>Sets maximum number of successive unsuccessful recovery attempts after which the output fails permanently. By default this option is set to 0 (unlimited).
<dt><b>recovery_wait_time</b> <i>duration</i>
<dd>Waiting time before the next recovery attempt after previous unsuccessful recovery attempt. Default value is 5 seconds.
<dt><b>recovery_wait_streamtime</b> <i>bool</i>
<dd>If set to 0 (false), the real time is used when waiting for the recovery attempt (i.e. the recovery will be attempted after at least recovery_wait_time seconds). If set to 1 (true), the time of the processed stream is taken into account instead (i.e. the recovery will be attempted after at least <i>recovery_wait_time</i> seconds of the stream is omitted). By default, this option is set to 0 (false).
<dt><b>recover_any_error</b> <i>bool</i>
<dd>If set to 1 (true), recovery will be attempted regardless of type of the error causing the failure. By default this option is set to 0 (false) and in case of certain (usually permanent) errors the recovery is not attempted even when <i>attempt_recovery</i> is set to 1.
<dt><b>restart_with_keyframe</b> <i>bool</i>
<dd>Specify whether to wait for the keyframe after recovering from queue overflow or failure. This option is set to 0 (false) by default.</dl>
 

 <i>Examples</i>
<dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>Stream something to rtmp server, continue processing the stream at real-time rate even in case of temporary failure (network outage) and attempt to recover streaming every second indefinitely. 

 <pre> ffmpeg -re -i ... -c:v libx264 -c:a aac -f fifo -fifo_format flv -map 0:v -map 0:a
 -drop_pkts_on_overflow 1 -attempt_recovery 1 -recovery_wait_time 1 <a HREF="rtmp://example.com/live/stream_name">rtmp://example.com/live/stream_name</a></pre></dl><h3>tee</h3>The tee muxer can be used to write the same data to several files or any other kind of muxer. It can be used, for example, to both stream a video to the network and save it to disk at the same time. 

 It is different from specifying several outputs to the <b>ffmpeg</b> command-line tool because the audio and video data will be encoded only once with the tee muxer; encoding can be a very expensive process. It is not useful when using the libavformat <font SIZE="-1">API</font> directly because it is then possible to feed the same packets to several muxers directly.
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>use_fifo</b> <i>bool</i>
<dd>If set to 1, slave outputs will be processed in separate thread using <b>fifo</b> muxer. This allows to compensate for different speed/latency/reliability of outputs and setup transparent recovery. By default this feature is turned off.
<dt><b>fifo_options</b>
<dd>Options to pass to fifo pseudo-muxer instances. See <b>fifo</b>.</dl>
 

 The slave outputs are specified in the file name given to the muxer, separated by '|'. If any of the slave name contains the '|' separator, leading or trailing spaces or any special character, it must be escaped (see <b>the ``Quoting and escaping'' section in the </b><a HREF="/docs/linux/man/1-ffmpeg-utils/">ffmpeg-utils</a><b>(1) manual</b>). 

 Muxer options can be specified for each slave by prepending them as a list of <i>key</i>=<i>value</i> pairs separated by ':', between square brackets. If the options values contain a special character or the ':' separator, they must be escaped; note that this is a second level escaping. 

 The following special options are also recognized:
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>f</b>
<dd>Specify the format name. Useful if it cannot be guessed from the output name suffix.
<dt><b>bsfs[/</b><i>spec</i><b>]</b>
<dd>Specify a list of bitstream filters to apply to the specified output.
<dt><b>use_fifo</b> <i>bool</i>
<dd>This allows to override tee muxer use_fifo option for individual slave muxer.
<dt><b>fifo_options</b>
<dd>This allows to override tee muxer fifo_options for individual slave muxer. See <b>fifo</b>. 

 It is possible to specify to which streams a given bitstream filter applies, by appending a stream specifier to the option separated by <tt>&quot;/&quot;</tt>. <i>spec</i> must be a stream specifier (see <b>Format stream specifiers</b>). If the stream specifier is not specified, the bitstream filters will be applied to all streams in the output. 

 Several bitstream filters can be specified, separated by ``,''.
<dt><b>select</b>
<dd>Select the streams that should be mapped to the slave output, specified by a stream specifier. If not specified, this defaults to all the input streams. You may use multiple stream specifiers separated by commas (<tt>&quot;,&quot;</tt>) e.g.: <tt>&quot;a:0,v&quot;</tt>
<dt><b>onfail</b>
<dd>Specify behaviour on output failure. This can be set to either <tt>&quot;abort&quot;</tt> (which is default) or <tt>&quot;ignore&quot;</tt>. <tt>&quot;abort&quot;</tt> will cause whole process to fail in case of failure on this slave output. <tt>&quot;ignore&quot;</tt> will ignore failure on this output, so other outputs will continue without being affected.</dl>
 

 <i>Examples</i>
<dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>Encode something and both archive it in a WebM file and stream it as MPEG-TS over <font SIZE="-1">UDP</font> (the streams need to be explicitly mapped): 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i ... -c:v libx264 -c:a mp2 -f tee -map 0:v -map 0:a
 &quot;archive-20121107.mkv|[f=mpegts]<a HREF="udp://10.0.1.255:1234/">udp://10.0.1.255:1234/</a>&quot;</pre><dt>&bull;
<dd>As above, but continue streaming even if output to local file fails (for example local drive fills up): 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i ... -c:v libx264 -c:a mp2 -f tee -map 0:v -map 0:a
 &quot;[onfail=ignore]archive-20121107.mkv|[f=mpegts]<a HREF="udp://10.0.1.255:1234/">udp://10.0.1.255:1234/</a>&quot;</pre><dt>&bull;
<dd>Use <b>ffmpeg</b> to encode the input, and send the output to three different destinations. The <tt>&quot;dump_extra&quot;</tt> bitstream filter is used to add extradata information to all the output video keyframes packets, as requested by the MPEG-TS format. The select option is applied to <i>out.aac</i> in order to make it contain only audio packets. 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i ... -map 0 -flags +global_header -c:v libx264 -c:a aac
 -f tee &quot;[bsfs/v=dump_extra]out.ts|[movflags=+faststart]out.mp4|[select=a]out.aac&quot;</pre><dt>&bull;
<dd>As below, but select only stream <tt>&quot;a:1&quot;</tt> for the audio output. Note that a second level escaping must be performed, as ``:'' is a special character used to separate options. 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i ... -map 0 -flags +global_header -c:v libx264 -c:a aac
 -f tee &quot;[bsfs/v=dump_extra]out.ts|[movflags=+faststart]out.mp4|[select=\'a:1\']out.aac&quot;</pre></dl>
 

 Note: some codecs may need different options depending on the output format; the auto-detection of this can not work with the tee muxer. The main example is the <b>global_header</b> flag.
<h3>webm_dash_manifest</h3>WebM <font SIZE="-1">DASH</font> Manifest muxer. 

 This muxer implements the WebM <font SIZE="-1">DASH</font> Manifest specification to generate the <font SIZE="-1">DASH</font> manifest <font SIZE="-1">XML.</font> It also supports manifest generation for <font SIZE="-1">DASH</font> live streams. 

 For more information see:
<dl COMPACT><dt>&bull;
<dd>WebM <font SIZE="-1">DASH</font> Specification: &lt;<b><a rel="nofollow" HREF="https://sites.google.com/a/webmproject.org/wiki/adaptive-streaming/webm-dash-specification">https://sites.google.com/a/webmproject.org/wiki/adaptive-streaming/webm-dash-specification</a></b>&gt;
<dt>&bull;
<dd><font SIZE="-1">ISO DASH</font> Specification: &lt;<b><a rel="nofollow" HREF="http://standards.iso.org/ittf/PubliclyAvailableStandards/c065274_ISO_IEC_23009-1_2014.zip">http://standards.iso.org/ittf/PubliclyAvailableStandards/c065274_ISO_IEC_23009-1_2014.zip</a></b>&gt;</dl>
 

 <i>Options</i> 

 This muxer supports the following options:
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>adaptation_sets</b>
<dd>This option has the following syntax: ``id=x,streams=a,b,c id=y,streams=d,e'' where x and y are the unique identifiers of the adaptation sets and a,b,c,d and e are the indices of the corresponding audio and video streams. Any number of adaptation sets can be added using this option.
<dt><b>live</b>
<dd>Set this to 1 to create a live stream <font SIZE="-1">DASH</font> Manifest. Default: 0.
<dt><b>chunk_start_index</b>
<dd>Start index of the first chunk. This will go in the <b>startNumber</b> attribute of the <b>SegmentTemplate</b> element in the manifest. Default: 0.
<dt><b>chunk_duration_ms</b>
<dd>Duration of each chunk in milliseconds. This will go in the <b>duration</b> attribute of the <b>SegmentTemplate</b> element in the manifest. Default: 1000.
<dt><b>utc_timing_url</b>
<dd><font SIZE="-1">URL</font> of the page that will return the <font SIZE="-1">UTC</font> timestamp in <font SIZE="-1">ISO</font> format. This will go in the <b>value</b> attribute of the <b>UTCTiming</b> element in the manifest. Default: None.
<dt><b>time_shift_buffer_depth</b>
<dd>Smallest time (in seconds) shifting buffer for which any Representation is guaranteed to be available. This will go in the <b>timeShiftBufferDepth</b> attribute of the <font SIZE="-1"><b>MPD</b></font> element. Default: 60.
<dt><b>minimum_update_period</b>
<dd>Minimum update period (in seconds) of the manifest. This will go in the <b>minimumUpdatePeriod</b> attribute of the <font SIZE="-1"><b>MPD</b></font> element. Default: 0.</dl>
 

 <i>Example</i> 

 <pre> ffmpeg -f webm_dash_manifest -i video1.webm \
 -f webm_dash_manifest -i video2.webm \
 -f webm_dash_manifest -i audio1.webm \
 -f webm_dash_manifest -i audio2.webm \
 -map 0 -map 1 -map 2 -map 3 \
 -c copy \
 -f webm_dash_manifest \
 -adaptation_sets &quot;id=0,streams=0,1 id=1,streams=2,3&quot; \
 manifest.xml</pre><h3>webm_chunk</h3>WebM Live Chunk Muxer. 

 This muxer writes out WebM headers and chunks as separate files which can be consumed by clients that support WebM Live streams via <font SIZE="-1">DASH.</font> 

 <i>Options</i> 

 This muxer supports the following options:
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>chunk_start_index</b>
<dd>Index of the first chunk (defaults to 0).
<dt><b>header</b>
<dd>Filename of the header where the initialization data will be written.
<dt><b>audio_chunk_duration</b>
<dd>Duration of each audio chunk in milliseconds (defaults to 5000).</dl>
 

 <i>Example</i> 

 <pre> ffmpeg -f v4l2 -i /dev/video0 \
 -f alsa -i hw:0 \
 -map 0:0 \
 -c:v libvpx-vp9 \
 -s 640x360 -keyint_min 30 -g 30 \
 -f webm_chunk \
 -header webm_live_video_360.hdr \
 -chunk_start_index 1 \
 webm_live_video_360_%d.chk \
 -map 1:0 \
 -c:a libvorbis \
 -b:a 128k \
 -f webm_chunk \
 -header webm_live_audio_128.hdr \
 -chunk_start_index 1 \
 -audio_chunk_duration 1000 \
 webm_live_audio_128_%d.chk</pre><h2>Metadata</h2>FFmpeg is able to dump metadata from media files into a simple UTF-8-encoded INI-like text file and then load it back using the metadata muxer/demuxer. 

 The file format is as follows:
<dl COMPACT><dt>1.
<dd>A file consists of a header and a number of metadata tags divided into sections, each on its own line.
<dt>2.
<dd>The header is a <b>;FFMETADATA</b> string, followed by a version number (now 1).
<dt>3.
<dd>Metadata tags are of the form <b>key=value</b>
<dt>4.
<dd>Immediately after header follows global metadata
<dt>5.
<dd>After global metadata there may be sections with per-stream/per-chapter metadata.
<dt>6.
<dd>A section starts with the section name in uppercase (i.e. <font SIZE="-1">STREAM</font> or <font SIZE="-1">CHAPTER</font>) in brackets (<b>[</b>, <b>]</b>) and ends with next section or end of file.
<dt>7.
<dd>At the beginning of a chapter section there may be an optional timebase to be used for start/end values. It must be in form <b>TIMEBASE=</b><i>num</i><b>/</b><i>den</i>, where <i>num</i> and <i>den</i> are integers. If the timebase is missing then start/end times are assumed to be in milliseconds. 

 Next a chapter section must contain chapter start and end times in form <b>START=</b><i>num</i>, <b>END=</b><i>num</i>, where <i>num</i> is a positive integer.
<dt>8.
<dd>Empty lines and lines starting with <b>;</b> or <b>#</b> are ignored.
<dt>9.
<dd>Metadata keys or values containing special characters (<b>=</b>, <b>;</b>, <b>#</b>, <b>\</b> and a newline) must be escaped with a backslash <b>\</b>.
<dt>10.
<dd>Note that whitespace in metadata (e.g. <b>foo = bar</b>) is considered to be a part of the tag (in the example above key is <b>foo</b> , value is 
&nbsp;<b>bar</b>).</dl>
 

 A ffmetadata file might look like this: 

 <pre> ;FFMETADATA1
 title=bike\\shed
 ;this is a comment
 artist=FFmpeg troll team
 
 [CHAPTER]
 TIMEBASE=1/1000
 START=0
 #chapter ends at 0:01:00
 END=60000
 title=chapter \#1
 [STREAM]
 title=multi\
 line</pre>By using the ffmetadata muxer and demuxer it is possible to extract metadata from an input file to an ffmetadata file, and then transcode the file into an output file with the edited ffmetadata file. 

 Extracting an ffmetadata file with <i>ffmpeg</i> goes as follows: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i INPUT -f ffmetadata FFMETADATAFILE</pre>Reinserting edited metadata information from the <font SIZE="-1">FFMETADATAFILE</font> file can be done as: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i INPUT -i FFMETADATAFILE -map_metadata 1 -codec copy OUTPUT</pre><h2>Protocol Options</h2>The libavformat library provides some generic global options, which can be set on all the protocols. In addition each protocol may support so-called private options, which are specific for that component. 

 Options may be set by specifying -<i>option</i> <i>value</i> in the FFmpeg tools, or by setting the value explicitly in the <tt>&quot;AVFormatContext&quot;</tt> options or using the <i>libavutil/opt.h</i> <font SIZE="-1">API</font> for programmatic use. 

 The list of supported options follows:
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>protocol_whitelist</b> <i>list</i> <b>(</b><i>input</i><b>)</b>
<dd>Set a ``,''-separated list of allowed protocols. ``<font SIZE="-1">ALL''</font> matches all protocols. Protocols prefixed by ``-'' are disabled. All protocols are allowed by default but protocols used by an another protocol (nested protocols) are restricted to a per protocol subset.</dl><h2>Protocols</h2>Protocols are configured elements in FFmpeg that enable access to resources that require specific protocols. 

 When you configure your FFmpeg build, all the supported protocols are enabled by default. You can list all available ones using the configure option ``--list-protocols''. 

 You can disable all the protocols using the configure option ``--disable-protocols'', and selectively enable a protocol using the option &quot;--enable-protocol=<i></i><font SIZE="-1"><i>PROTOCOL</i></font><i></i>``, or you can disable a particular protocol using the option ''--disable-protocol=<i></i><font SIZE="-1"><i>PROTOCOL</i></font><i></i>&quot;. 

 The option ``-protocols'' of the ff* tools will display the list of supported protocols. 

 All protocols accept the following options:
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>rw_timeout</b>
<dd>Maximum time to wait for (network) read/write operations to complete, in microseconds.</dl>
 

 A description of the currently available protocols follows.
<h3>async</h3>Asynchronous data filling wrapper for input stream. 

 Fill data in a background thread, to decouple I/O operation from demux thread. 

 <pre> async:&lt;URL&gt;
 async:<a rel="nofollow" HREF="http://host/resource">http://host/resource</a>
 async:cache:<a rel="nofollow" HREF="http://host/resource">http://host/resource</a></pre><h3>bluray</h3>Read BluRay playlist. 

 The accepted options are:
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>angle</b>
<dd>BluRay angle
<dt><b>chapter</b>
<dd>Start chapter (1...N)
<dt><b>playlist</b>
<dd>Playlist to read (<font SIZE="-1">BDMV/PLAYLIST/</font>?????.mpls)</dl>
 

 Examples: 

 Read longest playlist from BluRay mounted to /mnt/bluray: 

 <pre> bluray:/mnt/bluray</pre>Read angle 2 of playlist 4 from BluRay mounted to /mnt/bluray, start from chapter 2: 

 <pre> -playlist 4 -angle 2 -chapter 2 bluray:/mnt/bluray</pre><h3>cache</h3>Caching wrapper for input stream. 

 Cache the input stream to temporary file. It brings seeking capability to live streams. 

 <pre> cache:&lt;URL&gt;</pre><h3>concat</h3>Physical concatenation protocol. 

 Read and seek from many resources in sequence as if they were a unique resource. 

 A <font SIZE="-1">URL</font> accepted by this protocol has the syntax: 

 <pre> concat:&lt;URL1&gt;|&lt;URL2&gt;|...|&lt;URLN&gt;</pre>where <i></i><font SIZE="-1"><i>URL1</i></font><i></i>, <i></i><font SIZE="-1"><i>URL2</i></font><i></i>, ..., <i></i><font SIZE="-1"><i>URLN</i></font><i></i> are the urls of the resource to be concatenated, each one possibly specifying a distinct protocol. 

 For example to read a sequence of files <i>split1.mpeg</i>, <i>split2.mpeg</i>, <i>split3.mpeg</i> with <b>ffplay</b> use the command: 

 <pre> ffplay concat:split1.mpeg\|split2.mpeg\|split3.mpeg</pre>Note that you may need to escape the character ``|'' which is special for many shells.
<h3>crypto</h3>AES-encrypted stream reading protocol. 

 The accepted options are:
<dl COMPACT><dt><b>key</b>
<dd>Set the <font SIZE="-1">AES</font> decryption key binary block from given hexadecimal representation.
<dt><b>iv</b>
<dd>Set the <font SIZE="-1">AES</font> decryption initialization vector binary block from given hexadecimal representation.</dl>
 

 Accepted <font SIZE="-1">URL</font> formats: 

 <pre> crypto:&lt;URL&gt;
 crypto+&lt;URL&gt;</pre><h3>data</h3>Data in-line in the <font SIZE="-1">URI.</font> See &lt;<b><a rel="nofollow" HREF="http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_URI_scheme">http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_URI_scheme</a></b>&gt;. 

 For example, to convert a <font SIZE="-1">GIF</font> file given inline with <b>ffmpeg</b>: 

 <pre> ffmpeg -i &quot;data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODdhCAAIAMIEAAAAAAAA//8AAP//AP///////////////ywAAAAACAAIAAADF0gEDLojDgdGiJdJqUX02iB4E8Q9jUMkADs=&quot; smiley.png</pre><h3>file</h3>File access protocol. 

 Read from or write to a file.
